subtopics.name: Increased intracranial pressure and head injury

questions.stem: A 70-year-old client had an ischemic stroke in the right cerebral hemisphere 2 days ago. The family says the client keeps trying to get out of bed alone. Which group of findings should the nurse expect with this stroke?

options.text: Right-sided weakness, aphasia and slow, cautious behavior
Left-sided weakness, impulsiveness and neglect of the left side
Right-sided weakness and trouble reading and writing
Weakness of both legs with loss of bladder control

rationale.correct: Right-brain stroke: left-sided weakness, neglect, impulsiveness and poor judgment, so safety is the main concern. Left-brain stroke: right-sided weakness, aphasia and slow, cautious behavior.

perOption.a: These occur with left hemisphere strokes.
perOption.b: Right hemisphere damage affects the left side, spatial awareness and judgment.
perOption.c: Language deficits usually come from left hemisphere damage.
perOption.d: This pattern suggests a spinal cord problem, not a hemispheric stroke.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Predict deficits after a right hemisphere stroke.

questions.stem: A client with expressive (Broca) aphasia after a left-sided stroke understands what is said but struggles to find words and becomes tearful. Which communication strategy is best?

options.text: Speak more loudly and slowly so each word is heard
Ask yes-or-no questions and offer a picture board
Finish the client's sentences to save frustration
Limit conversation until the speech has recovered

rationale.correct: Expressive aphasia: comprehension is intact but speech is not; give time and use simple questions and aids.

perOption.a: The client's hearing and understanding are not the problem.
perOption.b: These let the client communicate without needing fluent speech.
perOption.c: This can frustrate the client and discourage attempts to speak.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Communicate with a client who has expressive aphasia.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old client arrives at the emergency department with sudden right-sided weakness and slurred speech that began 1 hour ago. The glucose is 118 mg/dL. Which test should the nurse expect first?

options.text: Non-contrast CT scan of the head
MRI of the brain with gadolinium
Lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid
Carotid ultrasound of both sides

rationale.correct: Get a non-contrast head CT immediately to tell ischemic from hemorrhagic stroke.

perOption.a: A CT quickly rules out hemorrhage before thrombolytic therapy.
perOption.b: An MRI takes longer and is not the usual first test.
perOption.c: This is not the initial stroke test.
perOption.d: This is done later to find the cause.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the first diagnostic test for a suspected stroke.

questions.stem: A client with an acute ischemic stroke that began 90 minutes ago is a candidate for alteplase. The CT shows no bleeding, and the blood pressure is 196/112 mm Hg. What should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Starting the alteplase right away, since time is brain tissue
Lowering the pressure below 185/110 before alteplase
Bringing the pressure down to 120/80 within the hour
Holding the antihypertensives so the brain stays perfused

rationale.correct: Before alteplase, the blood pressure must be below 185/110; afterward, keep it below 180/105 for 24 hours.

perOption.a: Blood pressure must be below 185/110 before alteplase.
perOption.b: High blood pressure raises the risk of bleeding into the brain.
perOption.c: Rapid, deep lowering can extend the stroke.
perOption.d: This pressure is too high for thrombolysis.

references: American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: After a right-sided stroke, a client has left homonymous hemianopsia and leaves the food on the left half of the plate. Which intervention is most appropriate for long-term recovery?

options.text: Place the tray and call light on the client's left side
Teach the client to turn the head to scan to the left
Place a patch over the client's left eye during meals
Approach the client from the left so the client adapts

rationale.correct: Hemianopsia: place items in the intact field at first, and teach scanning toward the lost side.

perOption.a: The client cannot see the left visual field, so items there are missed.
perOption.b: Scanning makes up for the lost visual field.
perOption.c: Patching does not help hemianopsia.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with left-sided neglect after a stroke ignores the left arm, which often hangs off the wheelchair. Which intervention should the nurse include in the plan of care?

options.text: Dress the client's unaffected right side first each morning
Cue the client to look at the left arm and position it safely
Keep the left arm under the blanket so it stays warm
Avoid mentioning the arm, since the neglect will fade with time

rationale.correct: Unilateral neglect: cue the client to attend to the affected side and protect the limb.

perOption.a: The affected side is dressed first.
perOption.b: Cueing increases awareness and prevents injury to the neglected limb.
perOption.c: This increases neglect and the risk of injury.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching the family of a client at high risk for stroke. Which sudden signs should prompt the family to call 911? Select all that apply.

options.text: Loss of balance or coordination
Vision loss or double vision
Drooping of one side of the face
Weakness of one arm
Slurred or confused speech
Fever with chills
A headache that builds slowly over several days and eases with rest

rationale.correct: BE-FAST: Balance, Eyes, Face, Arm, Speech, Time to call 911.

perOption.a: B in BE-FAST: balance.
perOption.b: E: eyes.
perOption.c: F: face.
perOption.g: A gradual headache that eases is not a stroke warning sign; a sudden, severe one is.

references: American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach the warning signs of stroke.

questions.stem: A client admitted with a subdural hematoma is being monitored for increased intracranial pressure. Which finding is the earliest sign that the pressure is rising?

options.text: New restlessness and confusion about where the client is
Fixed and dilated pupils that do not react to light
Bradycardia with a widening pulse pressure on the monitor
Rigid extension of the arms and legs to pain

rationale.correct: A change in level of consciousness is the earliest sign of rising ICP.

perOption.a: A change in level of consciousness is the most sensitive early sign.
perOption.b: This is a late sign.
perOption.c: These are late signs (Cushing triad).
perOption.d: Decerebrate posturing is a late sign.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with a head injury has a blood pressure that has risen from 138/80 to 184/70 mm Hg, a heart rate that has fallen from 88 to 52/min, and irregular breathing. What do these findings indicate?

options.text: Cushing triad, a late sign of increased ICP
Hypovolemic shock from internal bleeding
Neurogenic shock from a cervical spine injury
Expected recovery as the swelling goes down

rationale.correct: Cushing triad: hypertension with a widening pulse pressure, bradycardia and irregular respirations; notify the provider at once.

perOption.a: A widening pulse pressure, bradycardia and irregular respirations signal impending herniation.
perOption.b: Shock causes hypotension and tachycardia.
perOption.c: Neurogenic shock causes hypotension with bradycardia.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with a traumatic brain injury has an intracranial pressure of 22 mm Hg. Which interventions help reduce the pressure? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep the head of the bed at 30 degrees
Keep the head and neck in a midline position
Avoid sharp flexion of the hips
Space out nursing care with rest periods
Place the client in Trendelenburg for a short time
Encourage the client to cough hard every hour

rationale.correct: Lower ICP by promoting venous drainage and avoiding activities that raise intrathoracic or abdominal pressure.

perOption.a: This promotes venous drainage from the brain.
perOption.b: Turning the head can block the jugular veins.
perOption.c: Hip flexion raises abdominal and intracranial pressure.
perOption.d: Clustering many activities can raise ICP.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with cerebral edema after a traumatic brain injury is receiving IV mannitol every 6 hours. The serum osmolality this morning is 328 mOsm/kg, and urine output has been 250 mL/hr. What should the nurse do before the next dose?

options.text: Give the dose as scheduled, since the output shows it is working
Hold the dose and notify the provider of the osmolality
Give the dose faster to reduce the time the client has a full bladder
Restrict oral and IV fluids until the next dose is given

rationale.correct: Mannitol: monitor osmolality (hold if above about 320 mOsm/kg), urine output, electrolytes and signs of heart failure, and use an in-line filter.

perOption.a: An osmolality above about 320 mOsm/kg means the next dose may cause dangerous dehydration.
perOption.b: Mannitol is usually held when the osmolality is above about 320 mOsm/kg because of the risk of kidney injury and dehydration.
perOption.c: Changing the rate does not address the high osmolality.
perOption.d: Restricting fluids would worsen the dehydration.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old client injured in a fall from a ladder has clear fluid draining from the nose and bruising behind both ears. The client needs gastric decompression. Which action should the nurse avoid?

options.text: Inserting a nasogastric tube
Checking the drainage for a halo sign on gauze
Raising the head of the bed to 30 degrees
Notifying the provider of the drainage

rationale.correct: Basal skull fracture: Battle sign, raccoon eyes and CSF leak; nothing is passed through the nose, and an orogastric tube is used instead.

perOption.a: These findings suggest a basal skull fracture; a tube through the nose can enter the brain.
perOption.b: A halo on gauze suggests CSF and is appropriate to check.
perOption.c: This is appropriate.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Avoid nasal tubes in suspected basal skull fracture.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old was knocked out for about a minute after being hit in the temple by a baseball, then woke, talked normally and said only that the head ached. Two hours later, the client is hard to wake and has a dilated right pupil. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Epidural hematoma
Concussion
Chronic subdural hematoma
Migraine with aura

rationale.correct: An epidural hematoma is a neurosurgical emergency; the lucid interval can be falsely reassuring.

perOption.a: A brief loss of consciousness, a lucid interval, then rapid decline is typical of arterial bleeding.
perOption.b: A concussion does not cause a delayed decline with pupil changes.
perOption.c: A chronic subdural develops over weeks.
perOption.d: This does not fit the picture.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a client 6 hours after a head injury. The client opens the eyes only when the nail bed is pressed, says random inappropriate words, and pulls the hand away from the painful stimulus. What is the client's Glasgow Coma Scale score?

rationale.correct: Eye opening to pain = 2. Verbal: inappropriate words = 3. Motor: withdraws from pain = 4. Total = 9.
references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Calculate a Glasgow Coma Scale score.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old with a mild concussion from a football tackle is being discharged from the emergency department with a parent. Which statement shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll come back if I keep vomiting or my headache gets worse."
"My mom will stay with me and wake me tonight as instructed."
"I can play in Saturday's game if I feel fine by then."
"I'll take it easy at school and limit screen time for now."

rationale.correct: Concussion: watch for red flags, rest, and return to activity gradually with clearance.

perOption.a: These are warning signs.
perOption.b: Observation is recommended.
perOption.c: Return to contact sports needs a gradual plan and medical clearance.
perOption.d: Cognitive rest early on is appropriate.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach a client after a concussion.

questions.stem: A client with epilepsy has had one tonic-clonic seizure after another for 6 minutes without waking in between. The nurse has turned the client on the side and given oxygen. IV access is in place, and the glucose is 104 mg/dL. Which medication should the nurse prepare to give first?

options.text: IV lorazepam
Oral phenytoin
IV levetiracetam
Rectal acetaminophen

rationale.correct: Status epilepticus: protect the airway, give a benzodiazepine (IV lorazepam, or IM midazolam), then a second-line drug.

perOption.a: A benzodiazepine is first-line for status epilepticus.
perOption.b: Oral drugs cannot be given during a seizure.
perOption.c: This is second-line, given after a benzodiazepine.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse witnessed a client's seizure from start to finish. Which documentation is most useful to the provider?

options.text: When it began and ended, what moved and how the client was after
The time the seizure started and the name of the nurse who saw it
What the client ate and drank in the 4 hours before the seizure
Which family members were present when the seizure happened

rationale.correct: Document onset, duration, progression, type of movements, level of consciousness, incontinence and the post-ictal state.

perOption.a: These details help identify the seizure type and guide treatment.
perOption.b: This is not enough information.
perOption.c: This is not the key data.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing a loading dose of IV phenytoin for a client with recurrent seizures. The client has a peripheral IV with D5W running. Which action is correct?

options.text: Flush the line with saline and give it no faster than 50 mg/min
Add the phenytoin to the running D5W bag so that it is diluted
Give it by deep IM injection to avoid irritating the client's vein
Push it rapidly over 1 minute to stop seizures sooner

rationale.correct: IV phenytoin: saline only, a slow rate, an in-line filter, and cardiac and blood pressure monitoring.

perOption.a: Phenytoin is compatible only with saline; a rapid infusion can cause hypotension and dysrhythmias.
perOption.b: Phenytoin precipitates in dextrose.
perOption.c: IM phenytoin is erratically absorbed and damages tissue.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client taking phenytoin 100 mg three times a day has a level of 28 mcg/mL (therapeutic range 10 to 20). The client recently started fluconazole. Which findings should the nurse expect?

options.text: Nystagmus, an unsteady gait and slurred speech
Increased alertness and difficulty sleeping
A sudden rise in blood pressure
Unintended weight loss and frequent loose stools

rationale.correct: Phenytoin toxicity: nystagmus, ataxia, slurred speech and confusion; many drugs, such as fluconazole, raise levels.

perOption.a: These are signs of phenytoin toxicity.
perOption.b: Toxicity causes sedation.
perOption.c: This is not typical.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old client has started levetiracetam after a first seizure. Which statement by the client shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll tell my provider if I feel depressed or think about hurting myself."
"I'll stop taking it once I've gone a month without a seizure."
"I won't drive until my provider tells me it's safe."
"I may feel drowsy for the first couple of weeks."

rationale.correct: Never stop antiseizure drugs suddenly; watch for mood changes and suicidal thoughts.

perOption.a: Antiseizure drugs carry a warning about mood changes and suicidal thoughts.
perOption.b: Stopping suddenly can trigger seizures, including status epilepticus.
perOption.c: Driving restrictions apply.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach a client about antiseizure medication.

questions.stem: A college student has a fever of 39.4 °C, a severe headache and a stiff neck. When the nurse flexes the client's neck, the client's hips and knees flex. What does this finding indicate?

options.text: A positive Brudzinski sign, suggesting meningeal irritation
A positive Babinski sign, suggesting damage to the brain itself
A positive Romberg test, suggesting a balance problem
A normal reflex response in a young adult

rationale.correct: Signs of meningeal irritation: nuchal rigidity, Brudzinski sign and Kernig sign.

perOption.a: This finding suggests meningitis.
perOption.b: The Babinski sign involves the toes fanning out when the sole is stroked.
perOption.c: The Romberg test checks balance.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with confirmed meningococcal meningitis has been on droplet precautions since IV ceftriaxone was started yesterday at 1400. The family asks when they can visit without masks. What should the nurse tell them?

options.text: "When the precautions end, 24 hours after the antibiotics were started."
"Once the client has finished the full 7-day course of IV antibiotics at home."
"Masks are not needed, because meningitis does not spread to visitors."
"Not until a repeat lumbar puncture shows the fluid is clear."

rationale.correct: Meningococcal meningitis: droplet precautions until 24 hours of effective antibiotics; close contacts may need prophylaxis.

perOption.a: Droplet precautions for meningococcal disease continue until 24 hours of effective antibiotics.
perOption.b: Precautions do not need to last the full course.
perOption.c: Meningococcus spreads by respiratory droplets.
perOption.d: A repeat lumbar puncture is not required to end precautions.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with suspected meningitis is about to have a lumbar puncture at the bedside. How should the nurse position the client?

options.text: Side-lying, knees drawn up, chin tucked
Prone, with a pillow under the head and chest
Supine, with the arms at the sides
Sitting upright with the back straight

rationale.correct: Lumbar puncture: fetal position, or sitting and leaning forward; afterward, encourage fluids and watch for headache.

perOption.a: Curving the spine widens the spaces between the vertebrae.
perOption.b: This does not open the spaces.
perOption.c: This does not give access.
perOption.d: Sitting is possible only when leaning forward to curve the spine.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Position a client for a lumbar puncture.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing four clients with brain injuries in the neuro ICU. Which response to a painful stimulus indicates the most severe brain dysfunction?

options.text: Rigid extension of the arms and legs with the wrists turned outward
Bending of the arms toward the chest with the legs extended
Reaching toward the site of the painful stimulus to try to push it away
Opening the eyes and squeezing the nurse's hand when asked

rationale.correct: Decerebrate (extension) posturing is worse than decorticate (flexion) posturing.

perOption.a: Extension (decerebrate) posturing indicates brainstem damage and a worse prognosis.
perOption.b: Flexion (decorticate) posturing indicates damage higher in the brain and is less severe.
perOption.c: Localizing to pain is a purposeful response.
perOption.d: Following commands is a normal response.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A 58-year-old client with poorly controlled hypertension calls the clinic nurse. Highlight the findings that require emergency evaluation for a possible hemorrhagic stroke.

segments.text: a sudden, severe headache, "the worst of my life"
taking blood pressure medicine this morning

rationale.correct: A sudden, severe headache with vomiting and neck stiffness needs emergency evaluation for hemorrhage.

perOption.s2: A thunderclap headache suggests subarachnoid hemorrhage.
perOption.s4: Vomiting with a sudden headache suggests raised ICP.
perOption.s6: Blood in the subarachnoid space irritates the meninges.
perOption.s10: This is not an alarming finding.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
